title: On Attention, 'Cognitive Endurance' and Reading
author: Doug Lemov
summary: Doug Lemov argues that the smartphone era has taught educators something valuable: attention is malleable, and that insight should reshape how reading is taught. Drawing on his own forthcoming book on the science of reading, he argues that classrooms can deliberately rebuild students' attentional capacity by structuring reading experiences around sustained, focused, connected engagement rather than fragmented tasks. He then presents a striking NBER working paper by Christina Brown and colleagues on 'cognitive endurance as human capital': a field experiment with 1,600 Indian primary school students who were randomly given more time in sustained cognitive activity during the school day showed 22% less performance decline over time during intellectual tasks, suggesting effortful thinking itself builds the capacity to sustain effortful thinking. Lemov highlights the study's equity dimension -- poorer students both fatigue faster and attend schools offering fewer opportunities to practise sustained thinking -- and draws two practical conclusions: reading classrooms need more actual sustained reading time built into the habit of the room, and schools need reliable, orderly, low-disruption environments, since 'cognitive endurance' can't be practised amid constant low-level interruption.
points: Lemov's framing -- the smartphone proved attention is malleable, so it can be deliberately rebuilt, not just protected -- reverses the usual doom-laden narrative about phones and attention into an argument for intentional classroom design.

The NBER field experiment's core finding (22% less performance decline from more sustained cognitive-activity time) is unusually strong causal evidence, not correlational, for the claim that practising sustained focus itself builds the capacity for sustained focus.

Lemov's flag on the equity dimension -- poorer students both fatigue faster and get fewer opportunities to build cognitive endurance -- reframes 'cognitive endurance' as a resource unevenly distributed by wealth, not just an individual trait.

His second practical conclusion -- that orderly, low-disruption schools are a precondition for practising cognitive endurance -- links a seemingly unrelated behaviour-management argument directly to a specific cognitive-science mechanism.
quotes: Short version: if nothing else, the smartphone, having fractured the attention of millions, has taught us that attention is malleable.
We can re-build attention and empathy in part by causing students to engage in stretches of sustained and fully engaged reading.
We focus specifically on cognitive endurance: the ability to sustain effortful mental activity over a continuous stretch of time.
Using a field experiment with 1,600 Indian primary school students, we randomly increase the amount of time students spend in sustained cognitive activity during the school day.
This indicates that the experience of effortful thinking itself increases the ability to accumulate traditional human capital.

Globally and in the US, the poor exhibit cognitive fatigue more quickly than the rich across field settings; they also attend schools that offer fewer opportunities to practice thinking for continuous stretches.
